newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria plans tobacco, alcohol advertisement ban.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria plans tobacco, alcohol advertisement ban.

text.p: Bulgaria plans to ban tobacco and alcohol advertisements from television, radio, newspapers and billboards in a draft health law due to be voted by parliament this month which advertisers say will cause them huge losses.
"If this law comes into force, next year's advertising revenue will drop by more than 10 percent," the chairman of the Advertising Agency Association (AAA), Krassimir Gergov, told a seminar.

Under the law proposed by the Health Ministry to comply with World Health Organisation (WHO) rules, cigarette and alcohol advertising will be allowed only in stores specialising in the sale of these products.
Critics of the law say that most WHO member countries have left open loopholes like billboard advertising of these products.

"Losses from such a ban will be immense. In a situation where this country struggles for each penny, to divert million- dollar cash flows to other countries is absurd," said Misha Lukic, managing director of the Sofia partner office of Saatchi & Saatchi, which is owned by Britain's Cordiant Plc.
Revenue from cigarette and alcohol advertisements could be used to improve Bulgaria's health care system through health insurance funds, he added.
Last year's tobacco advertising spending in Bulgaria amounted to $3 million.
Advertising companies will have to change their policies, resorting to direct marketing which involves offering free packs of cigarettes, delegates to the seminar said.
"These ads do not prompt people to smoke but offer them a choice. People do not stop smoking because of a lack of ads," said Lukic.
Advertisers attending an annual meeting of some 40 major local and global companies, agreed to lobby parliament to adopt a milder version of the cigarette and alcohol advertisement ban.
Bulgaria is currently negotiating with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) the introduction of a tough financial regime, called a currency board, to restore confidence in its collapsing economy.
The IMF has twice postponed funding so far due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets.
